title: Dog-Trade Defenses Need Records Before Public Trust
excerpt: Claims about stolen pets, poison bait, and farm-raised dogs require police, court, and quarantine records. Public safety needs proof—and abolition by 2030.
body_html:
Families cannot protect pets or communities with slogans. They need records: police seizure reports, court judgments, veterinary quarantine documents, and traceable transport permits. The material available for this dispatch identifies no verified incident, named case, location, or official record proving claims about cyanide bait, pet-theft convictions, or dog farms. Those claims must not be dressed as fact.

Myths need records, not repetition

“Farm-raised dogs” is not proof of lawful origin. A credible supply chain would show ownership records, veterinary inspection, quarantine compliance, transport documentation, and slaughter oversight. Without those records, buyers cannot distinguish farmed animals from stolen companions or animals moved outside disease-control systems. That gap harms Vietnamese families who expect pets, roads, markets, and neighborhoods to remain safe.

Rabies leaves no room for casual enforcement

Rabies spreads when infected saliva enters bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. After possible exposure, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical care. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. World Health Organization guidance requires action before symptoms develop. Household exposure incidents and commercial transport risks are separate problems; both demand competent quarantine and enforcement.

Vietnamese communities can demand proof and protection

Public health targets and local enforcement measures do not equal complete abolition. SDE’s campaign sets a clear political demand: nationwide abolition by 2030, backed by transparent records, protection for families, and enforcement against illicit operators. Sign the national petition. Add your name to a public demand for action, then follow campaign updates on how that demand reaches decision-makers.
